question: What is the main danger if nurses forget to count surgical needles properly?

options.A: Increasing the cost of the surgical gloves
options.B: Causing immediate allergic reactions to suture material
options.C: Leaving a needle inside the patient's body
options.D: Delaying the start of the surgical operation

explanation: You've got this! Missing a needle count can lead to a retained item inside the patient, which causes serious pain and infection. Always count carefully! [learn more](GNS123_U5_T8#GNS123_U5_T8_h1)

question: Why is counting needles such an important duty for a nurse?

options.A: It speeds up the surgeon's work during complex procedures
options.B: It serves as a legal and physical safety barrier for the patient
options.C: It is only done to satisfy hospital administrative rules
options.D: It reduces the need to sterilize instruments after the case

explanation: Great job thinking about patient safety! Accurate counts protect your patient from harm and protect you and your team legally. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T8#GNS123_U5_T8_h1)

question: During surgery, who is mainly responsible for writing down the numbers called out during a count?
explanation: Spot on! The circulating nurse stays in the unsterile area to clearly document all the numbers called out by the scrub team. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T8#GNS123_U5_T8_h2)

question: Oh no! A scrub nurse receives a broken suture needle from the surgeon. What should they do first?

options.A: Ask the surgeon to replace the needle holder
options.B: Wait until the end of the operation to mention the break
options.C: Ensure all pieces of the broken needle are accounted for
options.D: Throw the broken pieces into the general waste bin

explanation: You are learning fast! Every single piece of a broken sharp must be found right away so nothing is left inside the patient. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T8#GNS123_U5_T8_h2)

question: When is the very first (baseline) needle count done during a procedure?

options.A: When the patient is rolling out of the recovery room
options.B: After the surgeon has closed the skin incision
options.C: Before the surgery begins during instrument setup
options.D: Only when an emergency X-ray is requested

explanation: Fantastic! We always do a baseline count before any cut is made so we know exactly what we started with. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T8#GNS123_U5_T8_h3)

question: Why do nurses perform multiple needle counts at different stages of one operation?

options.A: To follow hospital billing procedures for disposable items
options.B: To allow the surgeon time to review patient notes
options.C: To give the surgical team mandatory rest breaks
options.D: To catch and correct missing items before the wound is closed

explanation: Exactly! Checking at different milestones makes sure we catch any missing item while we can still easily find it. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T8#GNS123_U5_T8_h3)

question: What is the best way for nurses to physically handle needles during a count?

options.A: Glance quickly over the tray from a distance
options.B: Count only the full packs without opening them
options.C: Let the surgeon handle the items alone
options.D: Point to or touch each item individually as it is counted

explanation: You've got it! Touching or pointing to each item helps ensure nothing gets skipped. Safety first! [learn more](GNS123_U5_T8#GNS123_U5_T8_h4)

question: Why is the final skin closure count so tricky if everyone is tired?

options.A: The anesthesia machine might lose electrical power
options.B: The hospital will run out of disposable suture packs
options.C: A missing item can easily be overlooked when fatigue sets in
options.D: The surgeon will finish the operation too quickly

explanation: Well reasoned! Long surgeries cause fatigue, making it extra important to stay sharp during the final count. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T8#GNS123_U5_T8_h4)

question: What is the very first thing a nurse must do if a needle count is incorrect?

options.A: Inform the surgeon and stop wound closure
options.B: Clean up the operating room and send the patient away
options.C: Wait until the patient wakes up to ask if they feel pain
options.D: Write an incident report and leave the theatre

explanation: Brilliant clinical thinking! Never let a wound be closed when a count is wrong. Always speak up right away. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T8#GNS123_U5_T8_h5)

question: If a needle is missing after a big surgery, what is the next step the team should take?

options.A: Ignore the discrepancy if the patient looks stable
options.B: Assume the needle evaporated and finish stitching the skin
options.C: Ask the patient to pay for a replacement needle
options.D: Perform a thorough search of the room and take an X-ray

explanation: Spot on! A missing needle means a full search of the room and an X-ray to confirm where it went. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T8#GNS123_U5_T8_h5)

question: Where should the final results of surgical needle counts be officially written down?

options.A: On the hospital notice board outside the theatre
options.B: In the personal diary of the scrub nurse
options.C: On a scrap piece of paper to be thrown away later
options.D: In the patient's intraoperative nursing record

explanation: Correct! Official notes go straight into the patient's permanent medical chart to keep records clear and safe. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T8#GNS123_U5_T8_h6)

question: Why are accurate nursing records about needle counts so important in a court of law?

options.A: They show how fast the surgical team can work
options.B: They prove that standard safety protocols were followed
options.C: They help the hospital calculate patient food bills
options.D: They determine the salary of the operating theatre staff

explanation: You're doing great! Clear charting is your best legal protection, proving you did your job safely and correctly. [learn more](GNS123_U5_T8#GNS123_U5_T8_h6)
